{{DISPLAYTITLE:Physics tools, in plain language}}
{{Research Toolkit map}}
''For anyone curious. What a physics tool is for, one small example taken from a law all the way to numbers, which tool answers which question, and what [[The Principia Machina|the Principia Machina]] does with a tool's answer. You do not need to follow any equation to read this page. Operators have [[The Principia Machina/Tools/Operator's guide|their own guide]], and AI agents [[The Principia Machina/Agent/Tools|their own page]]. All three start from [[The Principia Machina/Tools|the front page]]. The tools are one part of the [[The Principia Machina/Research Toolkit|Research Toolkit]], which also covers how to do the research and how an AI should go about it.''

== 1 Three jobs between an idea and a number ==

A physical theory starts as an idea and has to end as a number someone can measure. Between the two lie three jobs. People did all three by hand for centuries: Kepler ''found'' his laws in Tycho Brahe's tables of planet positions; Lagrange and Hamilton showed how to ''derive'' the equations of motion from a single quantity, the action ([[Hamilton's principle]]); and astronomers ''solved'' those equations, line by line, to predict where a planet would be.

The tools on these pages are computer programs for the same three jobs, and one tool, added in October 2026, does a fourth: it checks a step of the reasoning by machine.

* '''Find''': look at data and find the rule behind it.
* '''Derive''': start from a rule and work out the equations it implies.
* '''Solve''': start from the equations and work out the numbers.
* '''Check''': have a machine confirm that a step of the argument really follows.

<graphviz>

digraph jobs {
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#eaecf0", color="#a2a9b1", fontcolor="#202122ff", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10]; edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#54595d", fontcolor="#202122ff"];
  rankdir=TB;
  D [label="DATA\nmeasurements,\nobservations", shape=folder];
  A [label="A RULE\nthe action: one quantity\nthat sums up the system", fillcolor="#cedff2"];
  E [label="EQUATIONS\nhow each part moves", fillcolor="#cedff2"];
  N [label="NUMBERS\na prediction you can measure", fillcolor="#cef2e0"];

  D -> A [label="FIND\nPySR, AI Feynman,\nPySINDy, Lagrangian networks", color="#ac6600", fontcolor="#ac6600"];

  E -> N [label="SOLVE\nFEniCS, Devito, Dedalus, DeepXDE, FiPy, Clawpack,\nEinstein Toolkit, SpECTRE, QuTiP, Modelica", color="#14866d", fontcolor="#14866d"];
  N -> D [label="COMPARE\nonly at the\nvery end", style=dashed, constraint=false];
  CK -> A [style=dotted, arrowhead=none]; CK -> E [style=dotted, arrowhead=none];
}
</graphviz>

The dashed arrow matters. A prediction is compared with a measurement only after the work is done, never while it is being done. Section 6 explains why.

== <span id="pendulum"></span>2 One example, all the way through: a pendulum ==

A weight on a string, swinging. Here is the whole road from rule to number, once, so the rest of the page has something to hang on.

'''The rule.''' The action of a pendulum is built from two energies: the energy of motion and the energy of height. Written out, with ''m'' the mass, ''&ell;'' the string's length, ''g'' gravity and ''&theta;'' the angle from straight down:
:<math>L = \tfrac{1}{2} m \ell^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + m g \ell \cos\theta</math>

'''Derived.''' Hamilton's principle turns that one line into the equation of motion. A symbolic tool such as [[The Principia Machina/Tools/Cadabra2|Cadabra2]] or [[The Principia Machina/Tools/ModelingToolkit|ModelingToolkit.jl]] does this step the way a physicist does it on paper:
:<math>\ddot{\theta} = -\frac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta</math>
Notice that the mass has dropped out. The tool did not decide that; the mathematics did.

'''Solved.''' For small swings the equation has a famous answer: the time for one full swing is
:<math>T \approx 2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}</math>
For a string 1 m long (about 3.3 ft) and ''g'' = 9.81 m/s&sup2;, that is 2.006 seconds. For bigger swings there is no such short formula, and a solver steps the equation forward in time instead. It gives 2.038 s for a swing of 0.5 radian (about 29&deg;) and 2.139 s for 1 radian (about 57&deg;). The short formula is 1.6 per cent too fast at 29&deg; and 6 per cent too fast at 57&deg;.

'''Found, the other way round.''' Hand a tool such as [[The Principia Machina/Tools/PySR|PySR]] a long table of measured angles and times, and it can search for the equation that reproduces the table, and find <math>\ddot{\theta} = -(g/\ell)\sin\theta</math> without being told it.

<graphviz>
// The pendulum, through the three jobs.
digraph pendulum {
  rankdir=TB; node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#eaecf0", color="#a2a9b1", fontcolor="#202122ff", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10]; edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#54595d", fontcolor="#202122ff"];
  R [label="THE RULE\nenergy of motion and energy of height\nL = (1/2) m l^2 (dtheta/dt)^2 + m g l cos(theta)", fillcolor="#cedff2"];
  Q [label="THE EQUATION\nd2theta/dt2 = -(g/l) sin(theta)\n(the mass drops out)", fillcolor="#cedff2"];
  S [label="SMALL SWINGS\nT = 2 pi sqrt(l/g)\n= 2.006 s for 1 m", fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  B [label="BIG SWINGS\nstep the equation in time\n2.038 s at 29 degrees\n2.139 s at 57 degrees", fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  T [label="A TABLE OF SWINGS\nangle against time,\nmeasured", shape=folder];
  R -> Q [label="derive\nCadabra2 or ModelingToolkit.jl"];
  Q -> S [label="solve by hand\n(an approximation)"];
  Q -> B [label="solve by machine\nModelingToolkit.jl or Modelica"];
  T -> Q [label="find\nPySR or AI Feynman", color="#ac6600", fontcolor="#ac6600"];
  B -> T [label="compare, at the end", style=dashed];
}
</graphviz>

== 3 Solving a field: five ways to cut up space ==

A pendulum has one moving part. A field, such as the electromagnetic field in a cavity or a wave crossing a room, has a value at every point of space. A computer cannot hold infinitely many points, so each solver cuts space up in its own way. That choice is most of what separates the field solvers on these pages.

* '''A regular grid''' ([[The Principia Machina/Tools/Devito|Devito]]): space as graph paper. Each point looks at its neighbours to estimate how fast the field changes. Fast and simple; best for waves in simple boxes.
* '''A mesh of small shapes''' ([[The Principia Machina/Tools/FEniCS|FEniCS]]): space tiled with triangles or tetrahedra that follow curved walls. The action is added up shape by shape.
* '''Cells that trade with their neighbours''' ([[The Principia Machina/Tools/FiPy|FiPy]], [[The Principia Machina/Tools/Clawpack|Clawpack]]): space as boxes, and whatever leaves one box enters the next, so nothing is created or lost by rounding. Clawpack also follows sharp fronts, such as shocks.
* '''No grid at all''' ([[The Principia Machina/Tools/DeepXDE|DeepXDE]]): a neural network is bent until the field it describes obeys the equations everywhere at once.
* '''A sum of smooth waves''' ([[The Principia Machina/Tools/Dedalus|Dedalus]]): the field written as a sum of simple wave shapes, very accurate when the field is smooth.

<graphviz>
// Five ways a field solver cuts up space.
digraph cuts {
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#eaecf0", color="#a2a9b1", fontcolor="#202122ff", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10]; edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#54595d", fontcolor="#202122ff"];
  rankdir=LR;
  F [label="A FIELD\na value at\nevery point\n(infinitely many)", fillcolor="#cedff2"];
  G [label="GRID: graph paper; neighbours\nestimate change -- Devito", fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  M [label="MESH: triangles that follow\ncurved walls -- FEniCS", fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  V [label="CELLS: what leaves one box\nenters the next -- FiPy, Clawpack", fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  N [label="NO GRID: a neural network bent\nto obey the equations -- DeepXDE", fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  S [label="SMOOTH WAVES: a sum of simple\nwave shapes -- Dedalus", fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  F -> G [label="finite difference"]; F -> M [label="finite element"]; F -> V [label="finite volume"]; F -> N [label="physics-informed network"]; F -> S [label="spectral"];
}
</graphviz>

Four more solvers work in worlds of their own: the [[The Principia Machina/Tools/EinsteinToolkit|Einstein Toolkit]] and [[The Principia Machina/Tools/SpECTRE|SpECTRE]] solve the equations of general relativity, where space and time themselves move; [[The Principia Machina/Tools/QuTiP|QuTiP]] solves quantum systems that leak into their surroundings; and [[The Principia Machina/Tools/Modelica|Modelica]] solves machines made of connected parts, such as linkages and circuits, where there is no field at all.

The survey gives each tool a score out of ten for four kinds of work: actions, fields, relativity, and quantum systems or data. The scores are the survey's own judgments, not measurements; the [[The Principia Machina/Tools#The survey's scores at a glance|front page]] charts all eighty-eight of them. The ten tools added in October 2026 were scored by a different hand from the original twelve, as that page explains.

== 5 What the Principia Machina does with a tool's answer ==

The Principia Machina is a way of doing research with AI so that anyone can check the result afterwards. A tool's answer is never taken on the tool's word. It goes through the same steps as every other finding.

# '''It is written down as a numbered entry''' in the [[The Principia Machina/Walk through/3 The register: every finding, in order|register]] of a research container, with its steps and its starting assumptions spelled out, and the conditions it was worked under (for the pendulum: the string length, the starting angle).
# '''A machine checks its form''', not its physics: that every field is filled in, that the units agree, that the fingerprints of the text match. The server, TPX, never runs the physics tool.
# '''Another AI redoes it''' from the same starting point, without being shown the first answer. If both agree, the finding gains support; if not, the disagreement is logged in public.
# '''Only then is it compared with the world''': a measured value from outside is set beside it, and the difference is written down. Agreement is never claimed in words; the numbers speak.

<graphviz>
// A tool's answer, from the tool to the public record.
digraph answer {
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#eaecf0", color="#a2a9b1", fontcolor="#202122ff", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10]; edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#54595d", fontcolor="#202122ff"];
  rankdir=TB;
  T [label="A TOOL'S ANSWER\non someone's own computer", fillcolor="#ffedad"];
  R [label="1 A NUMBERED ENTRY\nsteps, assumptions, conditions written out", fillcolor="#cedff2"];
  C [label="2 FORM CHECKED\nfields, units, fingerprints (TPX)"];
  W [label="THE REGISTER\non the wiki, public", shape=box3d, fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  P [label="3 REDONE\nby another AI, not shown the answer", fillcolor="#cedff2"];
  V [label="4 COMPARED\nwith a measurement, after the work", fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  T -> R -> C -> W; W -> P [label="a match adds support;\na mismatch is logged"]; W -> V [label="the difference\nis recorded"];
}
</graphviz>

== 6 Why the answer is not shown the target ==

If you know the answer you want, it is easy to steer a calculation towards it without meaning to: a slightly different mesh here, a different starting guess there. So the Principia Machina keeps the measured value out of sight until the derivation is finished. It calls this ''benchmark quarantine''. A tool that was fitted to a set of data cannot then be tested against that same data: that would be grading a student with the answer key it studied from.

<graphviz>
// Benchmark quarantine: the measured value stays behind the wall until the work is done.
digraph quarantine {
  rankdir=LR; node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#eaecf0", color="#a2a9b1", fontcolor="#202122ff", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10]; edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#54595d", fontcolor="#202122ff"];
  subgraph cluster_work { label="WHILE THE WORK IS DONE"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=10; color="#a2a9b1";
    K [label="the kernel:\nlaws and assumptions", fillcolor="#cedff2"]; TO [label="the tool", fillcolor="#ffedad"]; RS [label="the result", fillcolor="#cef2e0"]; K -> TO -> RS; }
  WALL [label="QUARANTINE\nthe measured value\nis not used,\nnot aimed at", shape=box, fillcolor="#fee7e6"];
  M [label="the measured value\nfrom outside", shape=folder];
  CMP [label="the comparison:\nthe difference,\nwritten down", fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  M -> WALL [style=dashed, arrowhead=tee];
  RS -> CMP [label="after the\nlast step"]; M -> CMP [label="only now"];
}
</graphviz>

== 7 What a tool cannot do here ==

Each research container rests on a ''kernel'': the laws and assumptions everyone agreed to hold fixed for that piece of research ([[The Principia Machina/Walk through/2 The kernel: what you promise not to change|the walk through, page 2]]). A tool cannot change it. If a tool finds a better law in the data, that law does not slip into the old container. It becomes the starting point of a new one, with a new name, checked from the beginning and declared by a named person. The old container and everything in it stay exactly as they were.

<graphviz>
// A tool cannot change a kernel; a new law starts a new container.
digraph kernel {
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#eaecf0", color="#a2a9b1", fontcolor="#202122ff", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10]; edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#54595d", fontcolor="#202122ff"];
  rankdir=TB;
  TOOL [label="a tool finds a different\nlaw in the data", fillcolor="#ffedad"];
  NO [label="edit kernel A?\nREFUSED", fillcolor="#fee7e6"];
  OLD [label="CONTAINER A\nkernel A (fixed), its register", shape=box3d, fillcolor="#cef2e0"];
  NEW [label="CONTAINER B\nnew kernel, new name, checked\nfrom the start, declared by a person", shape=box3d, fillcolor="#cedff2"];
  TOOL -> NO [style=dashed]; TOOL -> NEW [label="the only way in"];
  OLD -> NEW [label="may be copied forward;\nA is never changed", style=dashed];
  { rank=same; NO; OLD; }
}
</graphviz>

A tool also cannot vouch for itself. A program can have bugs, and two runs of the same program share them. That is why the redo in step 3 is done by a different AI, and why the comparison in step 4 uses a measurement from outside. The ways of checking a tool's answer before anyone else does (units on every line, the easy limits, a second route to the same result, a machine-checked proof of a key step) are on the [[The Principia Machina/Research Toolkit/Research methods|research methods]] page.

== 8 A day's work, start to finish ==

{{#mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as The person in charge
  participant A as An AI agent
  participant T as A physics tool
  participant X as TPX, the server
  participant R as The register
  participant B as A second AI
  H->>A: work this container
  A->>T: solve the pendulum equation, start at 0.5 rad
  T-->>A: one full swing takes 2.038 s
  A->>A: write it up: steps, assumptions, conditions
  A->>X: here is the entry
  X->>X: check the form: fields, units, fingerprints
  X->>R: entry lands, numbered
  X->>B: redo this, from the same start
  B->>X: my result
  X->>R: match logged in public
|config.theme=neutral}}
